title: Advanced Git Log
description: Use git log with powerful filters, formats, and graphs to understand and search Git history.

data.text: git log is far more powerful than its default linear output suggests. With the right flags, you can filter by author, date, file, and message content; format output for scripts; and visualize the branch graph. Mastering git log turns your Git history from a list into a searchable, navigable record.

data.title: Common git log filters
items: **--author="name"** — Filter by author name or email
**--since="2 weeks ago"** — Filter by date range
**-- path/to/file** — Filter to commits touching a specific path
**-S"string"** — Find commits that added or removed a specific string

data.title: Filter git log by author, date, and file
data.code:
# Commits by a specific author in the last month
git log --author="Jane" --since="1 month ago" --oneline

# Commits that touch a specific file
git log --oneline -- src/auth/LoginService.cs

# Commits mentioning 'auth' in the message
git log --grep="auth" --oneline

# Find when a string was added or removed
git log -S"NullReferenceException" --oneline

# Combine multiple filters
git log --author="Jane" --since="1 month ago" --grep="fix" --oneline

data.text: Searching for when a string was introduced
The -S (pickaxe) flag finds commits where the specified string's presence in the diff changed. This is more powerful than grep because it searches the diff, not just the commit message.

data.title: Find when a specific error was introduced
data.code:
# Find the commit that introduced 'UnauthorizedAccessException'
git log -S"UnauthorizedAccessException" --oneline

# Find when a specific function was added
git log -S"public User GetUser(int id)" --oneline

# Combine with --all to search all branches
git log --all -S"obsolete-function" --oneline

# Show the actual diff
git log -p -S"UnauthorizedAccessException"

data.text: The --graph flag renders an ASCII branch graph. Combine it with --oneline and --all for a compact view of the entire repository topology.

data.title: Visualize branch history
data.code:
# Compact branch graph
git log --all --oneline --graph --decorate

# Graph with author and date
git log --all --graph --pretty=format:'%h %an %ad %s' --date=short

# Graph limited to last 20 commits
git log --oneline --graph --decorate -20

# Graph showing merges only
git log --oneline --graph --merges --decorate -20

data.text: Use --pretty=format to customize log output for scripts, reports, or dashboards. Common placeholders include %h (short hash), %an (author), %ad (date), %s (subject), and %b (body).

data.title: Custom log format for changelogs
data.code:
# Changelog-friendly format
git log --pretty=format:'- %s (%an, %ad)' --date=short

# CSV format for spreadsheets
git log --pretty=format:'%h,%an,%ad,%s' --date=short --no-merges

# JSON-like format for scripts
git log --pretty=format:'{"hash":"%h","author":"%an","date":"%ad","message":"%s"}' --date=short

# One-line with decorations (branch/tag names)
git log --oneline --decorate --all

data.title: Use git log aliases
data.text: Add aliases to your git config for commonly used log commands. For example: git config --global alias.lg 'log --oneline --graph --all --decorate'. Now git lg shows the full branch graph.
The --merges flag shows only merge commits. Combine it with --grep to find merges related to specific features or pull requests.

data.title: Find merge commits for a feature
data.code:
# Find merges from feature/auth branch
git log --merges --grep="feature/auth" --oneline

# Find merges into main
git log main --merges --oneline

# Find merges that touched a specific file
git log --merges -- src/auth/LoginService.cs --oneline

items.question: What is the difference between -S and -G in git log?
items.answer: -S (pickaxe) searches for commits where the count of a string changed in the diff. -G uses a regex on the diff. Use -G when you need pattern matching rather than exact string matching.

items.question: Can git log show deleted files?
items.answer: Yes. Use git log --all -- <path> where <path> is the path to a deleted file. Git tracks the path through history even after deletion.

items.question: Does git log follow renames?
items.answer: No by default. Use git log --follow <path> to follow renames. Note that --follow only tracks the most recent rename, not rename chains.

items.question: Can I search the body of commit messages?
items.answer: Yes. Use --grep for a substring search. Use -i for case-insensitive grep matching.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: git log supports powerful filters: --author, --since, --grep, -- path
-S searches for commits that added or removed a specific string
--graph visualizes the branch topology as an ASCII graph
--pretty=format customizes output for scripts and reports
Create git aliases for common log configurations
